title: Poles and zeros of a transfer function

sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
Factor a transfer function and the roots separate into zeros, from the numerator, and poles, from the denominator. Each pole \(p\) contributes a natural term \(e^{pt}\). A real pole at \(s=-a\) with \(a>0\) contributes \(e^{-at}\), which decays. A pole in the right half-plane grows, so the natural motion is unstable. The pole closest to the imaginary axis decays most slowly and usually dominates.

Zeros do not create natural terms. They set how strongly each term appears. A zero on top of a pole cancels that term. A zero in the right half-plane makes a step response start in the direction opposite its final value. A complex pair has a natural frequency and a damping ratio, and those two numbers are the second-order skill.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\[
H(s)=K\frac{\prod (s-z_i)}{\prod (s-p_k)},\qquad h(t)=\sum_k r_k e^{p_k t}
\]
A real pole at \(-a\) contributes \(e^{-at}\). Cancelling a factor \((s+a)\) that sits in both the numerator and the denominator removes that pole and that zero together.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: Take a single pole at \(s=-7\). The natural term is \(e^{-7t}\). At \(t=1\ \mathrm{s}\) it equals \(e^{-7}\approx 0.000912\). Now take \(H(s)=(s+8)/((s+8)(s+11))\). The zero at \(-8\) cancels the pole at \(-8\), and the natural motion that remains is \(e^{-11t}\). The cancelled pair does not add a second decay.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Reading stability from the zeros instead of the poles. Treating a cancelled pole-zero pair as if it still contributed \(e^{pt}\). Calling the imaginary part of a complex pole the whole story of that pole.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Pole and zero locations are the break points of a Bode plot. The natural frequency and damping ratio of a complex pair are read in the second-order skill.
